Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette:
Mai was 38 when the abuse began, a year into a relationship she had entered with the hope of building a family. Her partner, a man she had trusted, would become enraged over small things—a meal not ready on time, a mislaid set of keys. The worst incident happened in their kitchen. He accused her of hiding money, then slammed her against the counter, grabbed a chef’s knife from the block, and held it to her throat while screaming. She remembers the cold flat of the blade against her skin, the smell of oil and garlic, the way his knuckles whitened. But the memory comes in disconnected pieces—the knife, then the floor, then her own voice saying “please” without knowing if she actually spoke. The terror of that moment returns with photographic clarity, as if she is still pinned there, yet the sequences between images are missing. In the years since, she left that man, eventually married a kind accountant, and became a tutor, working one-on-one with students in their homes. But she has never shaken the belief that she has permanently changed for the worse—that the woman before that kitchen no longer exists. She feels like an outsider everywhere, even in her own marriage, certain that no one can ever understand what she carries, and that you can never know who will harm you.

Mai does not realize how much this belief shapes her memory until she is driving to a tutoring session. The sight of a man in a loose jacket on the sidewalk makes her stomach drop, and suddenly she is back in the kitchen, the knife-edge at her throat. The threat triggers the memory directly—her mind leaps from the stranger’s silhouette to the blade, as if the two are connected by a wire. Because she already believes she is permanently damaged, she interprets these intrusions not as ordinary flashbacks but as proof that she is broken beyond repair, that the event has rewritten her. That appraisal, in turn, makes the memories more frightening and more frequent; she expects them, dreads them, and so they come.

To cope, Mai has developed strategies that feel necessary but only tighten the cycle. Before entering a student’s home, she scans the front porch for anything that could be used as a weapon—a loose brick, a garden tool. She checks her rearview mirror obsessively while driving, even on empty streets, certain someone might be approaching. She is hypervigilant toward any person who seems aggressive or unpredictable, especially men who raise their voices. During a session, if a father walks past the room too quickly, Mai’s body reacts before her mind does—her shoulders tense, her breath shortens—and she begins scanning the room for potential weapons all over again. This constant monitoring ensures she notices every dangerous object: the letter opener on the desk, the kitchen knife visible through a half-open door. Each discovery reinforces her sense of threat, and that sense of threat sends her right back into the memory of the knife at her throat, as if the present and the past have fused.

Over the months, the cycle has worn her down. She has started canceling sessions with families who have male partners at home during the day, telling herself it is safer. Her husband has noticed she flinches when he reaches for a kitchen utensil, and she cannot explain why. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week: she was tutoring a fourteen-year-old boy, and he accidentally dropped a textbook with a loud slap on the table. Mai screamed, then apologized, then excused herself to the bathroom and wept. She is afraid she will lose her livelihood, and deeper still, she is afraid that the permanent damage is real—that she will never be able to stop seeing knives in every room. But she has come, because a small part of her still hopes that the woman she was before the kitchen exists somewhere, waiting to be found.
